{{short description|Byzantine philosopher, mathematician and logician}}
'''Leo the Mathematician''', '''the Grammarian''' or '''the Philosopher''' ({{langx|grc|Λέων ὁ Μαθηματικός}} or ὁ Φιλόσοφος, ''Léōn ho Mathēmatikós'' or ''ho Philósophos''; {{Circa|790}} &ndash; after January 9, 869<ref>Symeon the Logothete, ''Chronographia'' 132.4. Symeon the Logothete as well as the separate recension of the ''Chronographia'' written by Pseudo-Symeon the Logothete mentions that Leo survives the [[869 AD Earthquake of Byzantium]], which occurred during the Feast of St. Polyeuktos on January 9th, 869.</ref>) was a [[Byzantine philosophy|Byzantine philosopher]] and [[logician]] associated with the [[Macedonian Renaissance]] and the end of [[Byzantine Iconoclasm|the Second Byzantine Iconoclasm]]. His only preserved writings are some notes contained in manuscripts of [[Plato]]'s dialogues. He has been called a "true [[Polymath|Renaissance man]]"<ref name="rautman">Marcus Louis Rautman (2006), ''Daily Life in the Byzantine Empire'' (Greenwood Publishing Group, {{ISBN|0-313-32437-9}}), 294&ndash;95.</ref> and "the cleverest man in Byzantium in the 9th century".<ref>{{cite news|title=History of the Pianola|publisher=Pianola Institute|url=http://www.pianola.org/history/history_mechanical.cfm}}</ref> He was [[archbishop of Thessalonica]] and later became the head of the [[Magnaura|Magnaura School]] of philosophy in [[Constantinople]],<ref name="Holmes">{{Cite book | last1 = Holmes | first1 = George | title = The Oxford illustrated history of medieval Europe | year = 1990 | publisher = Oxford University Press | location = Oxford | isbn = 978-0-19-285435-3 | page = [https://archive.org/details/oxfordillustrate00holm/page/52 52] | url = https://archive.org/details/oxfordillustrate00holm/page/52 }}</ref> where he taught [[Organon|Aristotelian logic]].

== Life ==
Leo was born in [[Thessaly]], a cousin of the [[Patriarch of Constantinople]], [[John VII of Constantinople|John the Grammarian]]. Little is known about his early life.{{efn|There are speculations that Leo was of Armenian ancestry, but these claims have been challenged.{{sfn|Bromige|2023|p=22: "Shirinian identifies [...] Leo the Mathematician, as Armenian in origin, but these claims have been challenged"}} Leo, in fact, identified himself as a "[[Hellenes|Hellene]]".{{sfn|Casas Olea|2023|p=147}} There is a tendency amongst certain Byzantinists to propose an "Armenian" ancestry for certain Byzantine individuals and/or families with an obscure heritage as a "convenient solution",{{sfn|Bryer|1980|p=165}} even if the evidence is flimsy, non-existent or completely fictional.{{sfn|Kaldellis|2019|p=155-195}}}} In his youth he was educated at Constantinople, but found higher education options limited in the city and thus travelled to the monasteries of [[Andros, Greece|Andros]], where he could obtain rare manuscripts and was taught mathematics by an old monk.<ref name="browning">{{cite journal |last=Browning |first=Robert |year=1964 |title=Byzantine Scholarship |journal=Past and Present |issue=28 |pages=7–8 |doi=10.1093/past/28.1.3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Lemerle |first=Paul |title=Byzantine Humanism: The First Phase: Notes and Remarks on Education and Culture in Byzantium from Its Origins to the 10th Century |publisher=Brill |year=2017 |location=Leiden |pages=172 |language=English |translator-last=Helen |translator-first=Lindsay}}</ref> He originally taught privately in obscurity in Constantinople. The story goes that when one of his students<ref>According to the Pseudo-Symeon, this student was Boïditzes, who [[Sack of Amorium|betrayed]] [[Amorium]] to the caliph.</ref> was captured during the [[Byzantine–Arab Wars]], the [[Caliph of Baghdad|Caliph]] [[al-Mamun]] was so impressed by his knowledge of mathematics, providing proofs that his own scholars were unable to complete, and predictive abilities that he offered Leo great riches to come to [[Baghdad]].<ref>According to [[Joseph Genesius]] and [[Theophanes Continuatus]] between 829 and 833; Symeon the Logothete makes the caliph [[al-Mutasim]] and puts the invitation after the Islamic conquest of Amorium in the fall of 838, cf. {{cite journal |last=Treadgold |first=Warren T. |year=1979 |title=The Chronological Accuracy of the ''Chronicle'' of Symeon the Logothete for the Years 813&ndash;845 |journal=[[Dumbarton Oaks Papers]] |volume=33 |pages=162 |doi=10.2307/1291437|jstor=1291437 }}</ref> Leo took the letter from the caliph to the [[Byzantine emperor]] [[Theophilos (emperor)|Theophilos]], who, impressed by his international repute, conferred on him a school (''ekpaideutērion'') in either the Magnaura or the church of the [[Forty Martyrs of Sebaste|Forty Martyrs]].<ref>Symeon says the Magnaura, Continuatus the Forty Martyrs (Treadgold, "Chronological Accuracy ", 186).</ref>

In the version of the story recorded by [[Theophanes Continuatus]], the caliph, upon receiving Leo's letter of refusal, sent a letter requesting answers to some difficult questions of geometry and astrology, which Leo obliged. Al-Mamun then offered two thousands pounds of gold and a perpetual peace to Theophilos, if only he could borrow Leo's services briefly; the request was declined. The emperor then honoured Leo by having John the Grammarian consecrate him [[Metropolitan bishop|metropolitan]] of [[Thessalonica]], which post he held from the spring of 840 to 843. There is a discrepancy in this account, however, in that the caliph died in 833. It has been suggested that either the connection between the caliph's final letter and Leo's appointment as metropolitan is in error, or the caliph in question was actually al-Mutasim. This latter option squares with the account of [[Symeon the Logothete]], who makes Leo teach at the Magnaura from late 838 to early 840 and was paid handsomely.<ref>Treadgold, "Chronological Accuracy ", 172.</ref>

Leo, an iconoclast sometimes accused of paganism, lost his metropolitancy with the end of the [[Byzantine Iconoclasm|Iconoclasm]] in 843.<ref>Warren T. Treadgold (1997), ''A history of the Byzantine state and society'' (Stanford University Press), 447.</ref> Despite this, he delivered a sermon favourable of icons within months of Theophilos' death.<ref>Warren T. Treadgold (1988), ''The Byzantine Revival, 780&ndash;842'' (Stanford University Press), 372.</ref> Around 855, Leo was appointed at the head of a newly established Magnaura School by [[Bardas]].<ref>Treadgold, "Chronological Accuracy ", 187, believes, on the basis of the Logothete's account, that this occurred in 843 and was a re-founding of Theophilos' school.</ref> He was renowned for his philosophical, mathematical, medical, scientific, literary, philological, seismological, astronomic, and astrological learning, and was patronised by [[Theoktistos]] and befriended by [[Photios I of Constantinople]].<ref name="Tougher1997">{{cite book |title=The Reign of Leo VI (886&ndash;912): Politics and People |last=Tougher |first=Shaun |year=1997 |publisher=Brill |location=Leiden |isbn=90-04-10811-4 |page=113 }}</ref><ref name="Vlasto1970">{{cite book |title=The Entry of the Slavs into Christendom: An Introduction to the Medieval History of the Slavs |last=Vlasto |first=A. P. |year=1970 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |page=33 }}</ref> [[Saints Cyril and Methodius|Cyril]] was his student. Leo has been credited with a [[Byzantine beacon system|system of beacons]] (an optical telegraph) stretching across [[Asia Minor]] from [[Cilicia]] to Constantinople, which gave advance warning of Arab raids, as well as diplomatic communication.<ref name= "Holmes" /><ref name="Treadgold1979">{{cite journal |last=Treadgold |first=Warren T. |year=1979 |title=The Revival of Byzantine Learning and the Revival of the Byzantine State |journal=The American Historical Review |volume=84 |issue=5 |pages=1245–1266 [p. 1259] |doi=10.2307/1861467|publisher=American Historical Association |jstor=1861467 }}</ref> Leo also invented several [[automata]], such as trees with moving birds, roaring lions, and a levitating imperial throne.<ref name=rautman/> The throne was in operation a century later, when [[Liutprand of Cremona]] witnessed it during his visit to Constantinople.<ref name="Safran1998">{{cite book |title=Heaven on Earth: Art and the Church in Byzantium |last=Safran |first=Linda |year=1998 |publisher=Penn State Press |location=Pittsburgh |isbn=0-271-01670-1 |page=30 }} Records Liutprand's description.</ref><ref>For a detailed discussion of Leo's telegraph and his automata, see Leone Montagnini (2002), [http://www.armoniedeldisordine.it/opere.html#02i "Leone il Matematico, un anello mancante nella storia della scienza"], {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017235629/http://www.armoniedeldisordine.it/opere.html#02i |date=2013-10-17 }} ''Studi sull'Oriente Cristiano'', 6 (2), 89–108.</ref>

== Works ==
Most of Leo's writings have been lost. He wrote book-length works, poems, and many [[epigrams]],<ref>Among them are some centos preserved in the Palatine Anthology; see Prieto Domínguez, Óscar (2011), ''De Alieno Nostrum: el Centón profano en el mundo griego''. Estudios Filológicos, 328. Salamanca: Ediciones Universidad de Salamanca. {{ISBN|9788478002085}}, p. 120-179.</ref> and was also a compiler, who brought together a wide range of philosophical, medical, and astronomic texts. His library can at least partially be reconstructed: [[Archimedes]], [[Euclid]], [[Plato]], [[Paul of Alexandria]], [[Theon of Alexandria]], [[Proclus]], [[Porphyry (philosopher)|Porphyry]], [[Apollonius of Perga]], the lost ''Mechanics'' of Quirinus and Marcellus, and possibly [[Thucydides]].<ref name=browning/> He composed his own medical encyclopaedia. Later Byzantine scholars sometimes confused Leo with the scholar [[Leo Choirosphaktes]] and the emperor [[Leo VI the Wise]], and ascribe to him [[oracle]]s.

==Primary sources==
Recent years have seen the first translations into English of a number of primary sources about Leo and his times.
* Featherstone, Jeffrey Michael and Signes-Codoñer, Juan (translators). ''Chronographiae quae Theophanis Continuati nomine fertur Libri I-IV'' (Chronicle of [[Theophanes Continuatus]] Books I-IV, comprising the reigns of [[Leo V the Armenian]] to [[Michael III]]), Berlin, Boston: De Gruyter, 2015.
* Kaldellis, A. (trans.). ''On the reigns of the emperors'' (the history of [[Joseph Genesius|Joseph Genesios]]), Canberra: Australian Association for Byzantine Studies; Byzantina Australiensia 11, 1998.
* Ševčenko, Ihor (trans.). ''Chronographiae quae Theophanis Continuati nomine fertur Liber quo Vita Basilii Imperatoris amplectitur'' (Chronicle of [[Theophanes Continuatus]] comprising the Life of [[Basil I]]), Berlin: De Gruyter, 2011.
* Wahlgren, Staffan (translator, writer of introduction and commentary). ''The Chronicle of the Logothete'', Liverpool University Press; Translated Texts for Byzantinists, vol. 7, 2019.
* Wortley, John (trans.). ''A synopsis of Byzantine history, 811-1057'' (the history of [[John Scylitzes]], active 1081), Cambridge University Press, 2010.
